2 // ANNUAL REPORT 2025-26
Purpose of this report
This report covers the period from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. The Office of the
Independent Commissioner Against Corruption (OICAC) became part of the broader
Office of the Integrity and Ethics Commissioner (Integrity NT) on 1 June 2026. This
report therefore focusses on the work of the OICAC leading up to that change but
also refers to relevant aspects of the Integrity NT's work after that date. For ease of
reference, the report will primarily refer to OICAC.
The 2025-26 Annual Report of the Office of the Independent Commissioner Against
Corruption (OICAC) has been prepared to comply with annual reporting requirements under:
• section 128 of the Independent Commissioner Against Corruption Act 2017 (the ICAC Act)
• parts 3 and 9 of the Information Act 2002.
This annual report also highlights the performance of the OICAC in 2025-26 against approved
budget outputs and key performance measures as published in the Northern Territory
Government's 2025-26 Agency Budget Statements (Budget Paper no. 3).

Foreword: Commissioner
Shoyer
1 present the 2025-26 Annual Report of the Office of the Independent Commissioner Against Corruption (ICAC).
This reporting period has been one of significant transition and change. For the first eleven months of the year, the Office operated
under the leadership of two Acting Independent Commissioners Against Corruption before I commenced as Commissioner on 1
June 2026: Mr Greg Shanahan and Ms Naomi Loudon. During this time, the Office continued to deliver its statutory responsibilities
under the Independent Commissioner Against Corruption Act 2017 (NT) while also preparing for a new phase of organisational
reform and integration.
June 2026 saw the establishment of the Office of the Integrity and Ethics Commissioner (Integrity NT), bringing together
several Northern Territory integrity functions, including the ICAC, within a single organisation. As at the date of this report, the
agency remains in a period of transition and reorganisation. Significant work is underway to align systems, processes, governance
arrangements and resources across the newly amalgamated agency. This work is being undertaken with a clear objective: to
improve efficiency, strengthen capability and ensure public resources are used effectively, while maintaining the independence,
integrity and quality of work expected under the ICAC Act and the other legislation under my remit.
Despite these changes, the Office continued to deliver strong outcomes across its assessment, investigation, prevention and
engagement, legal, and review functions. During the year, the Office received a substantial volume of reports and allegations of
improper conduct, completed assessments within established timeframes, progressed complex investigations, delivered education
and prevention activities across the Northern Territory, and completed significant review work aimed at strengthening integrity
within public administration. The Office also continued to monitor and promote implementation of recommendations arising from
investigations and reviews.
The results achieved throughout 2025-26 reflect the professionalism, commitment and resilience of staff during a period of
considerable organisational change. I acknowledge the efforts of all staff who remained focused on delivering the Office's
statutory functions while adapting to new structures and ways of working. Their dedication has ensured that the Office continued
to provide independent oversight and support confidence in the integrity of public administration across the Northern Territory.
Looking ahead, my focus will be on building a strong and sustainable Integrity NT together with the Chief Executive Officer, Mr
Reece P Kershaw APM, that is equipped to meet future challenges while remaining firmly committed to the principles of integrity,
accountability, transparency and public trust.
The transition to the Office of the Integrity and Ethics Commissioner presents a significant opportunity to enhance the delivery
of integrity services across government and the wider community. I am confident that, through careful reform and continued
commitment to our legislative responsibilities, the organisation will be well placed to fulfil that role.
PSlu
Peter Shoyer
Integrity and Ethics Commissioner (as ICAC)

6 // ANNUAL REPORT 2025-26
Independent
Commissioner Against
Corruption
This report covers the period from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. The Office of the Independent Commissioner Against
Corruption (OICAC) became part of the broader Office of the Integrity and Ethics Commissioner (Integrity NT) on 1 June
2026. This report therefore focusses on the work of the OICAC leading up to that change but also refers to relevant
aspects of Integrity NT's work after that date. For ease of reference, the report will primarily refer to OICAC.
The Independent Commissioner Against Corruption (ICAC) has responsibility for discharging a range of statutory functions
prescribed in the ICAC Act.
Those functions are:
a) to identify and investigate improper conduct;
b) to protect persons who have assisted or may assist in detecting, preventing, investigating or otherwise responding to improper
conduct;
c) to prevent, detect and respond to improper conduct by:
developing and delivering education and training; and
auditing or reviewing practices, policies and procedures of public bodies and public officers; and
iii. developing and delivering advice, reports, information and recommendations; and
iv. referring matters to a referral entity for investigation or further investigation, disciplinary action or prosecution; and
v. making public comment;
vi. gathering intelligence about improper conduct;
d) to oversee and direct, as required, how referral entities deal with matters referred to them by the ICAC; and
e) to perform other functions conferred on the ICAC under the ICAC Act or another Act.
In discharging those functions, the ICAC is not subject to direction by any person in respect of the way statutory functions are
performed, or priority is given to any particular matter.
The Integrity and Ethics Commissioner (the IEC) holds office as the ICAC under the Integrity and Ethics Commissioner Act 2025. As
the principal integrity officer for the Northern Territory, the IEC brings together the functions of the Independent Commissioner
Against Corruption, Ombudsman, Information Commissioner and Health and Community Services Complaints Commissioner under
a single independent statutory office.

Executive
The Integrity and Ethics Commissioner (IEC) holds office as
the Independent Commissioner Against Corruption (ICAC)
and is responsible for exercising the statutory powers and
functions conferred under the ICAC Act. The Commissioner
is supported by Integrity NT, which is administered by a
Chief Executive Officer (CEO) who is responsible for the
agency's staffing, financial management and corporate
administration.
The CEO supports the IEC in exercising the functions and
powers of the ICAC and provides leadership and oversight
of the ICAC business units within Integrity NT. This
includes responsibility for investigations, assessments,
strategic intelligence and reviews, legal services,
prevention and engagement functions and corporate
services, ensuring the effective and independent delivery
of the Commissioner's statutory responsibilities.
Operations Unit
The Operations Unit is responsible for delivering the
assessment and investigation functions of the OICAC. The
unit supports the ICAC in undertaking statutory functions
by responding to reports, assessing information, and
conducting investigations into alleged improper conduct
involving public officers and public bodies.
Assessments
The Operations Unit is responsible for assessing all
reports received by the OICAC. Following assessment,
recommendations are made to the ICAC or delegate on
whether any action should be taken. The unit also reviews
responses from referral entities regarding actions taken in
response to referrals or preliminary inquiries initiated by
the ICAC.
Investigations
The Operations Unit supports the ICAC in investigating
allegations of improper conduct in accordance with the
ICAC Act. A range of investigative techniques are employed
to gather evidence, including the collection of business
and financial records, taking statements, conducting
interviews, and, where required, undertaking private
examinations.
Strategic Intelligence and Reviews
Unit
The Strategic Intelligence and Reviews Unit supports
the ICAC to deliver a range of functions. These functions
include gathering intelligence about improper conduct,
and evaluating or reviewing the practices, policies and
procedures of public bodies and public officers.
The unit also develops and delivers advice, reports,
information and recommendations.
Legal Unit
Through the General Counsel and legal staff, the Legal
Unit provides legal advice and support to the ICAC and
OICAC staff.
Legal Unit staff can act as counsel, assisting the ICAC
during private examinations.
The General Counsel and Legal Unit staff provide general
legal advice to the ICAC to assist in discharging statutory
functions by reviewing assessment and investigative
matters.
Legal Unit staff also provide advice on education and
prevention activities and support the ICAC to meet
strategic priorities.
Prevention and Engagement Unit
The Prevention and Engagement Unit delivers awareness,
engagement and prevention activities to public sector
agencies, local government councils and the community.
The unit develops prevention and engagement strategies
and resources and works with public bodies and public
officers to increase awareness of improper conduct and
foster a culture of reporting improper conduct in public
administration.
Corporate Services Unit
The Corporate Services Unit supports the operational
requirements of the OICAC by managing finance,
human resources, governance and risk. The Corporate
Services Unit works with other NT Government agencies
and external contractors to coordinate procurement,
work health and safety (WHS), records management,
information and communications, and technology support.
The unit also provides administrative and secretariat
services to the IEC, CEO and directors.

Section 18A of the ICAC Act states that the ICAC must not
investigate allegations of misconduct or unsatisfactory
conduct unless one of the considerations outlined in
subsection 18A(1)(a) or (b) of the ICAC Act is met.!
If, during the course of an investigation, the ICAC forms
the view that the likely outcome is a finding of no more
than misconduct or unsatisfactory conduct, then pursuant
to section 18A(2) the investigation must cease unless a
consideration under section 18A(1)(a) or (b) applies.
In accordance with section 128(2)(a) and (b) of the ICAC
Act, the ICAC is required to report the number of concluded
investigations by the ICAC of misconduct or unsatisfactory
conduct, including the number of concluded investigations
under section 18A(1)(a) or (b).

period under section 18A(1)(b). Operation Wattle was an
investigation into allegations that a Chief Executive Officer
failed to adequately manage a conflict of interest in regard
to a procurement process. No matters were concluded
under section 18A(1)(a).

The primary role of the Strategic Intelligence and Reviews
Unit is to conduct research and deliver analytical insights
that inform the ICAC's priorities and support the functions

Unit performance
Operation Banksia review
In September 2025, the former Acting Commissioner
Naomi Loudon commenced a review under section 23
of the ICAC Act, referred to as Operation Banksia, which
examined the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries'
(DAF), recruitment and selection practices, policies and
procedures.
The review considered recruitment and selection
processes of 10 advertised and 10 non-advertised positions
(e.g. expression of interest, contract extension and direct
appointment), reviewing adherence to legislation, policy,
delegations, determinations and the identification and
management of conflicts of interest.
On 26 February 2026, a draft review report was provided
to DAF for feedback, which included the findings and
proposed recommendations.
Overall, most recruitment activities were compliant and
demonstrated alignment with key merit-based principles.
However, several recurring gaps were identified that
presented improper conduct risks:
• Conflict of Interest management: Panels did not
evidence discussions of conflicts of interest prior
to shortlisting, declared relationships were not
consistently supported by management plans, and
referee and delegate conflict of interest declarations
were, at times, absent from selection reports.
• Merit integrity and recruitment controls: Inconsistent
practices were identified in verifying applicant
qualifications, approving job descriptions, maintaining
current merit selection training, documenting referee
checks, and ensuring appropriate panel balance in
terms of level and composition.
• Timeliness of recruitment processes: Advertised
recruitment processes showed extended timeframes
from commencement to finalisation, averaging 67 days
across the samples analysed.
• Delegate approval and governance oversight: Evidence
of delegate approval to fill vacancies was often unclear
or incomplete, with reliance on unsigned spreadsheets,
inconsistent records and a bulk email approval process
covering multiple recruitment actions.

DAF deliver training on conflicts of interest,

2. DAF update its internal guidance for expression of

3. DAF update the Human Resource delegations to

Training manual
b. that the merit selection training status of all

c. clear and consistent documenting of approvals
to fill a vacancy within the eRecruit system.
Recommendations were also made to the Office of the
Commissioner for Public Employment (OCPE) for whole of
government implementation as there were systemic issues
across the broader public service.
The recommendations made to the OCPE are:
OCPE update the whole of government recruitment
and selection templates, and corresponding policies,
procedures and guidelines, requiring the mandatory
conflict of interest declaration form to be completed
by the panel and signed by the delegate prior to
shortlisting, irrespective of whether any conflicts of
2. OCPE update the whole of government mandatory

b. a section requiring panels to provide documented
evidence of all pre-employment and suitability
checks performed, including confirmation that

The role of the ICAC Legal Unit is to provide legal advice to
the ICAC and OICAC staff.

discharge of statutory functions, direction in the collection

has oversight in the preparation of briefs of evidence for
referral to the Director of Public Prosecutions and NT
Police.

as counsel assisting the ICAC in examinations and is
responsible for coordinating referral of matters to external
counsel for legal advice.

relation to current Supreme Court decisions relevant to
ICAC operations.

ICAC in the discharge of statutory functions by:
• reviewing reports from the Assessments unit and
identifying matters for consideration regarding whether
to commence an investigation
• providing strategic guidance on education and
prevention activities
overseeing external litigation concerning the ICAC
• ensuring the Commissioner's strategic priorities are
being met.

develops, delivers and assists in the delivery of internal
and external training.

The Office of the ICAC compliance framework consisted of the following internal and external governance functions.
Internal governance
The Executive Committee met on a monthly basis and provided strategic advice and assistance to the ICAC in relation to:

• ensuring compliance with statutory and reporting requirements
• managing resources appropriated to the Office effectively and efficiently
• conducting investigations and taking action in accordance with the ICAC Act
• overseeing and managing organisational priorities and good corporate governance, including setting internal policies
• implementing and managing the Office of the ICAC's risk management framework, including responding to and treating work
health and safety matters
• reviewing and implementing recommendations from oversight bodies, such as the Audit, Risk and Compliance Committee
(ARCC) and from external stakeholders, including the Inspector of the ICAC, the Auditor-General and the Standing Committee
on the ICAC
• creating and maintaining a safe workplace
• leading and fostering a positive organisational culture
• assisting with any other matters determined by the ICAC.

reporting, internal control systems, risk management systems, and internal and external audit. The ARCC is headed by an external
chair.

The ARCC acts within its authority on behalf of the ICAC to:
• monitor the Office of the ICAC's risk registers, risk appetite statements and provide advice to the ICAC on management of risk
within the Office
• oversee the development and implementation of the Internal Audit Plan linked to the Office's risk registers
• review internal and external audit reports and oversee implementation of recommendations
• review public accountability disclosures, including financial and performance information in the Office's annual report, in line

Inspector of the ICAC
Mr Bruce McClintock SC was the Inspector of the ICAC
after being re-appointed to the role in November 2023 for
a term of 5 years. The Inspector is an independent officer
who provided oversight of the ICAC by delivering the
following functions:

evaluation to the ICAC Minister (the Chief Minister) and
the Legislative Assembly
• receiving and dealing with complaints about the ICAC or
ICAC staff members
• making recommendations to the ICAC (or other
public bodies) in relation to practices and procedures
concerning performance of the functions under the
ICAC Act.

entitled to full and free access to Office of the ICAC
premises and all items in the possession or control of the

members were obligated to provide reasonable assistance
to the Inspector.

136 of the ICAC Act and Evaluation of the ICAC pursuant
to section 135 of the ICAC Act. The Inspector provided this

in Parliament. There were no recommendations resulting

ceased, following the full commencement of the Integrity
and Ethics Commissioner Act 2025 (NT).
